anatomy.lede: Strip away the coat and a lion is almost indistinguishable from a tiger. What sets it apart is its social life — and the male's mane, a signal read by friend and rival alike.

hotspots.label: Jaws and canines
hotspots.text: Powerful jaws and teeth pull down and kill prey often much larger than the lion itself. Adults have 30 teeth.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Lions use visual cues to recognise one another — including reading the size and colour of a male's mane from a distance.

hotspots.label: Mane
hotspots.text: Only male lions grow manes, from about age three. A dark mane signals good nutrition and high testosterone.

hotspots.label: Forelegs
hotspots.text: Strong, compact bodies and powerful forelegs let lions wrestle large animals to the ground.

hotspots.label: Body
hotspots.text: Adult males typically weigh about 189 kg and females about 126 kg; the heaviest male on record weighed 272 kg.

hotspots.label: Tail tuft
hotspots.text: The long tail ends in a black tuft; cubs are born with spotted coats that fade as they grow.

senses.lede: Living in groups that come and go across a large territory, lions keep track of each other — and of rivals — by sound, sight and scent.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Lions listen closely to strangers' roars. In playback trials, pride females could judge how many intruders were calling and compared that with how many companions they had.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Manes are read visually: their length signals fighting ability to other males, and their darkness affects which males females choose.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: Resident males regularly spray vegetation with urine and scuff the ground to mark territory, and females spray occasionally.

body.lede: The lion's body reflects its role as a heavy, cooperative predator — and the costs of male showmanship.

systems.title: A hot coat
systems.text: Manes come at a price: dark-maned males run hotter, have more abnormal sperm and eat less in the hottest months. Males grow lighter or shorter manes in hotter seasons, years and places.

systems.title: Living with a virus
systems.text: In the Serengeti, Ngorongoro Crater and Kruger, 92% of lions tested carried feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV). It does not seem to harm lions, though it kills domestic cats.

systems.title: Built for big prey
systems.text: Lions mainly eat animals weighing about 45–450 kg, such as zebra and wildebeest. In lean times they switch to rodents, reptiles and other small animals.

genome.lede: A chromosome-level lion genome was published in 2020. Ancient and modern lion DNA now traces how the species spread and shrank.

findings.title: Cave lions split long ago
findings.text: Lions and the extinct cave lions of Ice Age Eurasia shared an ancestor about 500,000 years ago, and probably did not interbreed afterwards.

findings.title: Two modern lineages
findings.text: Living lions fall into two main lineages that split about 70,000 years ago, with later gene flow between them.

findings.title: Indian lions lack variety
findings.text: The lions of India's Gir Forest have almost no genetic diversity, the legacy of extremely small populations in the recent past.

mind.lede: The Serengeti lions have been studied continuously since 1966, making them among the best-understood social carnivores on Earth.

studies.title: Wings and centres
studies.text: In 486 group hunts in Etosha, Namibia, lionesses took set roles: some circled the prey as 'wings' while others waited as 'centres'. Each lioness tended to keep the same position, and hunts went best when they did.

studies.title: Counting the opposition
studies.text: When recorded roars of strange females were played in 21 pride territories, residents were less likely to approach when they were outnumbered — and roared to recruit absent pride members.

studies.title: What a mane says
studies.text: Dark-maned males in the Serengeti had longer reproductive lives and their cubs survived better. Females preferred dark manes, while rival males paid attention to mane length.

studies.title: Shared nurseries
studies.text: Related lionesses often give birth at the same time and nurse each other's cubs in a crèche, which lowers cub deaths.

survival.lede: Adult lions have no natural predators. Their dangers come from other lions, from hunger and from people.

tactics.title: Defending the territory together
tactics.text: Lions live at higher densities than other big cats, so pride members must defend their territory together against takeovers by other lions.

tactics.title: Coalitions of brothers
tactics.text: Young males leave home at about 2.5 years and team up, usually with brothers, to take over a pride. Coalitions of three or four tend to hold a pride for longer than pairs.

tactics.title: Stealing a meal
tactics.text: Lions scavenge actively, following hyenas and vultures, and steal kills from hyenas and leopards.

threats.title: Poison and snares
threats.text: Lions are killed with snares, rifles and arrows, and because they scavenge they are especially vulnerable to poisoned carcasses.

threats.title: Disease from dogs
threats.text: Many lions have died from diseases such as canine distemper, spread by domestic dogs from villages near their habitat.

threats.title: Declines across Africa
threats.text: Lion populations are falling across most of Africa; only some intensively managed southern populations are holding up.

life.lede: A lion's life is shaped by the pride: cubs are raised communally, and their survival depends on how long their fathers hold power.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: One to six cubs are born, each weighing 1–2 kg. Females usually have a litter every two years.

stages.name: Hidden cub
stages.text: Eyes open by about 11 days and cubs can run at a month old, but their mother keeps them hidden until about eight weeks.

stages.name: Pride cub
stages.text: Cubs are weaned at 7–10 months and depend on the pride until at least 16 months. Up to 80% die in their first two years, many from starvation or from males taking over the pride.

stages.name: Nomad or pride member
stages.text: Young females usually stay in their mother's pride for life. Young males are driven out and roam for two to three years before trying to win a pride of their own.

lifespan.value: Females 15–16 years in the wild; few males live past 10
